NCERT Ganita Manjari · Grade 9 · Part I

Chapter 1 — Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

Key Concepts · Exercise 1.1 & 1.2 · End-of-Chapter Solutions
Coordinate Plane Distance Formula Midpoint Formula Collinearity
What is this chapter about? Imagine you want to tell someone exactly where a point is on a flat sheet of paper — not "somewhere near the middle" but its exact spot. Coordinate geometry gives us a way to do this using just two numbers, written as \( (x, y) \). Every point on the page gets its own unique pair of numbers, the same way every house on a street gets its own address. In this chapter you'll learn how this address system works, how to measure the distance between two addresses (points), and how to find the point exactly halfway between two others.
Coordinate Plane — Basics ▾
Fig. 1.2 — Structure of the coordinate plane (NCERT)
Origin O = (0, 0) — where the x-axis and y-axis meet.
Point P = (x, y) — x is measured along the x-axis, y along the y-axis.
Points on the x-axis: y = 0. Points on the y-axis: x = 0.
Exam tip: Always write x first, y second. \( (3,5) \) and \( (5,3) \) are different points.
Quadrant Summary ▾
Fig. 1.4 — The four quadrants (NCERT)
QuadrantxyExample
I++(3, 5)
II−+(−4, 2)
III−−(−3, −5)
IV+−(2, −6)
Mirror in x-axis: \( (x,y)\to(x,-y) \). Mirror in y-axis: \( (x,y)\to(-x,y) \). If \(x=y\) then \((x,y)=(y,x)\); if \(x\neq y\) then \((x,y)\neq(y,x)\).

💡 Think and Reflect

  1. What is the x-coordinate of a point on the y-axis?
  2. Is there a similar generalisation for a point on the x-axis?
  3. Does point Q (y, x) ever coincide with point P (x, y)? Justify your answer.
  4. If \(x \neq y\), then \((x,y) \neq (y,x)\); and \((x,y) = (y,x)\) if and only if \(x = y\). Is this claim true?
(1) x-coordinate = 0, always. (2) Yes — the y-coordinate of a point on the x-axis is 0, always. (3) Only when x = y — then P and Q become the same point. (4) Yes, the claim is true: swapping x and y only gives the same point when they were already equal.
Distance Formula ▾
Fig. 1.6 — Triangle ADM (NCERT)
Fig. 1.7 — Deriving the distance AD (NCERT)
For \( A(x_1,y_1) \) and \( B(x_2,y_2) \):
\[ d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2} \]
Same y (horizontal line): distance \( = |x_2-x_1| \). Same x (vertical line): distance \( = |y_2-y_1| \). Squaring removes the sign, so distance always comes out positive.

💡 Think and Reflect

  1. In moving from A (3, 4) to D (7, 1), what distance has been covered along the x-axis? What about the distance along the y-axis?
  2. Can these distances help you find the distance AD?
(1) Along the x-axis: 4 units. Along the y-axis: 3 units. (2) Yes — together with the right angle at the corner they form, these two distances become the two legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is AD, so the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem gives us AD directly.
Fig. 1.9 — Triangle AMD reflected in the y-axis (NCERT)

💡 Think and Reflect

  1. What has remained the same and what has changed with this reflection?
  2. Would these observations be the same if ΔADM is reflected in the x-axis (instead of the y-axis)?
(1) Same: the side lengths (AD, DM, MA), the overall shape and size (congruent triangle), and the y-coordinates of every point. Changed: every x-coordinate flips sign, the triangle moves to a different quadrant, and its left-right orientation is mirrored.
(2) Similar but not identical — reflecting in the x-axis instead keeps all x-coordinates the same and flips the sign of every y-coordinate, mirroring the triangle top-to-bottom instead of left-right. Side lengths are still preserved either way.
Midpoint Formula ▾
The midpoint M of segment AB, where \( A(x_1,y_1) \) and \( B(x_2,y_2) \):
\[ M = \left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right) \]
To find a missing endpoint B when M and A are known: \( x_2 = 2M_x - x_1 \), \( y_2 = 2M_y - y_1 \).

Exercise Set 1.1 — Reiaan's Room (Fig. 1.3)

NCERTQ1(i)
The door \( D_1R_1 \) lies on the x-axis. How far is it from the y-axis? How far from the x-axis?
Fig. 1.3 — Reiaan’s room (NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9)
Ask yourself: Where does the door lie?
Given
\( D_1 = (8,0) \), \( R_1 = (11.5,0) \) — both lie on the x-axis.
Working
Distance from x-axis = y-coordinate of the door = 0 units (the door lies on the x-axis)
Distance from y-axis = x-coordinate of \( D_1 \) = 8 units
Answer
∴ Door is 8 units from the y-axis, and 0 units from the x-axis.
NCERTQ1(ii)
What are the coordinates of \( D_1 \)?
Fig. 1.3 — Reiaan’s room (NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9)
Answer
∴ \( D_1 = (8,0) \)
NCERTQ1(iii)
If \( R_1 = (11.5,0) \), how wide is the door? Is this a comfortable width for a wheelchair user?
Fig. 1.3 — Reiaan’s room (NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9)
Ask yourself: How do we find the width of a door lying on the x-axis?
Given
\( D_1 = (8,0) \), \( R_1 = (11.5,0) \) — same y, so width = difference of x-coordinates.
Formula
Two points on the same horizontal line: width \( = |x_2-x_1| \)
Working
Width = 11.5 − 8 = 3.5 units
1 unit = 1 foot, so width = 3.5 ft
Convert feet to inches: 3.5 × 12 = 42 inches
A wheelchair needs about 32 inches (≈ 2.7 ft) of clear width
3.5 ft > 2.7 ft (door width exceeds minimum requirement)
Answer
∴ Width = 3.5 units. This is comfortable — a wheelchair user can enter easily.
NCERTQ1(iv)
\( B_1(0,1.5) \) and \( B_2(0,4) \) are the ends of the bathroom door. Is it narrower or wider than the room door?
Fig. 1.3 — Reiaan’s room (NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9)
Ask yourself: Both \( B_1 \) and \( B_2 \) have x = 0. What does that tell us?
Given
\( B_1(0,1.5) \), \( B_2(0,4) \) — both have x = 0, so they lie on the y-axis; width = difference of y-coordinates.
Formula
Two points on the same vertical line: width \( = |y_2-y_1| \)
Working
Width of bathroom door = 4 − 1.5 = 2.5 units
Width of room door = 3.5 units
2.5 < 3.5
Answer
∴ The bathroom door (2.5 units) is narrower than the room door (3.5 units).

💡 Think and Reflect

  1. What are the standard widths for a room door? Look around your home and in school.
  2. Are the doors in your school suitable for people in wheelchairs?
These are for you to check yourself — go measure a door at home or school and compare it to what you found in Q1(iii)!

Exercise Set 1.2 — Reiaan's Room (Fig. 1.5)

NCERTQ1(i)
Three feet of a study table are at \( (8,9) \), \( (11,9) \), \( (11,7) \). Where is the fourth foot?
💡 The table, drawn right where it sits in the room — can you spot where the 4th foot (?) should go?
Ask yourself: What shape is a table? What do we know about its corners?
Given
A = (8,9), B = (11,9), C = (11,7). A table is rectangular — opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Working
A and B have the same y = 9 (AB is a horizontal side)
B and C have the same x = 11 (BC is a vertical side)
Fourth point D needs the same x as A, so x = 8
Fourth point D needs the same y as C, so y = 7
D = (8, 7)
Answer
∴ The fourth foot of the table is at (8, 7).
NCERTQ1(iii)
What is the width and length of the table? Can the height be found from this figure?
The completed table, drawn to scale in the room, with width and length labeled
Formula
Same y → width \( = |x_2-x_1| \). Same x → length \( = |y_2-y_1| \)
Working
Width: between (8,9) and (11,9) — same y, subtract x: 11 − 8 = 3 units
Length: between (11,9) and (11,7) — same x, subtract y: 9 − 7 = 2 units
Height cannot be found — this is a 2-D top view; height runs upward, out of the plane
Answer
∴ Width = 3 units, Length = 2 units. Height cannot be determined from this 2-D figure.
NCERTQ2
The bathroom door is hinged at \( B_1 \) and opens into the bedroom. Will it hit the wardrobe?
Ask yourself: When a door opens, what path does it sweep?
Given
\( B_1 = (0,1.5) \), \( B_2 = (0,4) \). A door opening sweeps a curved path (an arc) — think of the door tracing part of a circle as it swings, with the hinge at the centre and the door's width as the radius.
Working
Door width = 4 − 1.5 = 2.5 units (radius of the swept arc)
Wardrobe starts at x = 3
Distance from \( B_1 \) to wardrobe = 3 units
2.5 < 3
Answer
∴ The door will NOT hit the wardrobe. If made wider than 3 units, it may — then it should open inward into the bathroom instead.
NCERTQ3(i)
What are the coordinates of the four corners O, F, R, P of the bathroom?
The bathroom rectangle O–F–R–P highlighted in blue on the actual room photo
Answer
∴ O = (0,0), F = (0,9), R = (−6,9), P = (−6,0)
NCERTQ3(ii)
What is the shape of the showering area SHWR? Write the coordinates of its four corners.
Fig. 1.5 — Reiaan’s room, extended (NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9)
Given
S = (−6,6), H = (−3,6), W = (−2,9), R = (−6,9)
Working
SH: y = 6 for both (horizontal side, length 3)
RW: y = 9 for both (horizontal side, length 4)
SH ≠ RW, but SH ∥ RW (one pair of parallel sides, unequal length)
Answer
∴ SHWR is a trapezium. Corners: S(−6,6), H(−3,6), W(−2,9), R(−6,9).
📌 Trapezium: a four-sided shape (quadrilateral) with exactly one pair of opposite sides parallel.
NCERTQ4(i)
The dining room is 18 ft × 15 ft, its length running from P to A. Find the coordinates of its corners.
The photo extended downward — the dining room (dashed) attaches right below the existing room along P–A
Given
P = (−6,0), A = (12,0) — from the figure. Length = 18 ft, width = 15 ft, room extends downward.
Working
Length PA = 12 − (−6) = 12 + 6 = 18 ft (matches given length)
Width = 15 ft, extending in the negative y direction
Bottom corners: (12, −15) and (−6, −15)
Answer
∴ Dining room corners: P(−6,0), A(12,0), Q(12,−15), S(−6,−15)
NCERTQ4(ii)
A rectangular 5 ft × 3 ft dining table is placed exactly at the centre of the dining room. Find the coordinates of its feet.
The dining table, drawn to scale at the centre of the dining room, with all 4 feet and the centre point labeled
Ask yourself: How do we find the centre of a rectangle?
Given
Room spans x: −6 to 12, y: −15 to 0. Table size: 5 units along x, 3 units along y.
Formula
\[ \text{Centre} = \left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right) \]
Working
Centre x = \( \dfrac{-6+12}{2} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3 \)
Centre y = \( \dfrac{0+(-15)}{2} = \dfrac{-15}{2} = -7.5 \)
Half-length = 5/2 = 2.5, Half-width = 3/2 = 1.5
Corner 1: (3 − 2.5, −7.5 − 1.5) = (0.5, −9)
Corner 2: (3 + 2.5, −7.5 − 1.5) = (5.5, −9)
Corner 3: (3 + 2.5, −7.5 + 1.5) = (5.5, −6)
Corner 4: (3 − 2.5, −7.5 + 1.5) = (0.5, −6)
Answer
∴ Feet of dining table: (0.5,−9), (5.5,−9), (5.5,−6), (0.5,−6)

End-of-Chapter Exercises

NCERTQ1
What are the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of the point of intersection of the two axes?
Answer
∴ x-coordinate = 0, y-coordinate = 0. Point of intersection = (0, 0).
NCERTQ2
Point W has x-coordinate \( -5 \). Predict the coordinates of point H on the line through W parallel to the y-axis. Which quadrants can H lie in?
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Ask yourself: If a line is parallel to the y-axis, what stays the same for every point on it?
Working
A line parallel to the y-axis keeps the same x-coordinate for every point on it
So H = (−5, y) for any y
If y > 0: H is in Quadrant II (x < 0, y > 0)
If y < 0: H is in Quadrant III (x < 0, y < 0)
If y = 0: H is on the x-axis
Answer
∴ H = (−5, y). H can lie in Quadrant II, Quadrant III, or on the x-axis.
NCERTQ3(i)
Points R(3,0), A(0,−2), M(−5,−2), P(−5,2) form quadrilateral RAMP. Find two sides that are perpendicular.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
📌 Quadrilateral: any four-sided closed shape. "RAMP" here just names the four corners in order — R to A to M to P back to R.
Working
AM: A(0,−2) to M(−5,−2) — both have y = −2 (horizontal line)
MP: M(−5,−2) to P(−5,2) — both have x = −5 (vertical line)
A horizontal line is always perpendicular to a vertical line
Answer
∴ \( AM \perp MP \). These two sides are perpendicular to each other.
NCERTQ3(ii)
Find one side of RAMP that is parallel to one of the axes.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Answer
∴ AM is parallel to the x-axis (same y = −2). MP is parallel to the y-axis (same x = −5).
NCERTQ3(iii)
Find two points of RAMP that are mirror images of each other. Which axis?
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Working
Compare M(−5,−2) and P(−5,2)
Same x-coordinate: −5
y-coordinates: −2 and +2 — equal size, opposite sign
Flipping over the x-axis sends \( (x,y) \) to \( (x,-y) \) (exactly this pattern)
Answer
∴ M and P are mirror images of each other in the x-axis.
NCERTQ4
Plot Z(5,−6). Construct a right-angled triangle IZN and find the lengths of all three sides.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Ask yourself: How can we form a right-angled triangle easily, starting from just one point?
Given
Z = (5,−6). Choose I = (5,0) on the x-axis and N = (0,−6) on the y-axis, so that the right angle falls at Z.
📌 Hypotenuse: the longest side of a right-angled triangle — it's always the side opposite the right angle. Here, that's IN.
Formula
\[ IN = \sqrt{(5-0)^2+(0-(-6))^2} \]
Working
IZ: same x = 5 (vertical). ZN: same y = −6 (horizontal). So \( IZ \perp ZN \), right angle at Z
\( IZ = |0-(-6)| = 6 \) units
\( ZN = |5-0| = 5 \) units
\( IN = \sqrt{5^2+6^2} = \sqrt{25+36} = \sqrt{61} \) units
Answer
∴ IZ = 6 units, ZN = 5 units, IN = \( \sqrt{61} \) units. (Other valid choices of I and N give different lengths.)
NCERTQ5
What would a system of coordinates be like if we did not have negative numbers? Would it let us locate all points in the 2-D plane?
Working
Without negatives, coordinates can only be 0 or positive
Only Quadrant I, the positive axes, and the origin can be reached
Quadrants II, III, IV would all be unreachable
Answer
∴ No. Without negative numbers we could only locate points in Quadrant I; the other three quadrants and the negative axes would be inaccessible.
NCERTQ6
Are the points M(−3,−4), A(0,0), G(6,8) on the same straight line? Suggest a method without plotting.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Ask yourself: How can we check three points lie on the same line, without plotting them?
📌 Collinear points: three or more points that lie on the same straight line.
Given
Three points are collinear if the distance between the two outer points equals the sum of the distances from each outer point to the middle one.
Formula
\[ d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2} \]
Working
\( MA = \sqrt{(0-(-3))^2+(0-(-4))^2} = \sqrt{3^2+4^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \)
\( AG = \sqrt{(6-0)^2+(8-0)^2} = \sqrt{6^2+8^2} = \sqrt{36+64} = \sqrt{100} = 10 \)
\( MG = \sqrt{(6-(-3))^2+(8-(-4))^2} = \sqrt{9^2+12^2} = \sqrt{81+144} = \sqrt{225} = 15 \)
Check: \( MA + AG = 5+10 = \textcolor{#B03030}{15} \), and \( MG = \textcolor{#B03030}{15} \)
Answer
∴ MA + AG = MG, so M, A and G are collinear — they lie on the same straight line.
NCERTQ7
Use the method from Q6 to check if R(−5,−1), B(−2,−5), C(4,−12) are on the same straight line.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Working
\( RB = \sqrt{(-2-(-5))^2+(-5-(-1))^2} = \sqrt{3^2+(-4)^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \)
\( BC = \sqrt{(4-(-2))^2+(-12-(-5))^2} = \sqrt{6^2+(-7)^2} = \sqrt{36+49} = \sqrt{85} \)
\( RC = \sqrt{(4-(-5))^2+(-12-(-1))^2} = \sqrt{9^2+(-11)^2} = \sqrt{81+121} = \sqrt{202} \)
\( \sqrt{85} \approx 9.22 \)
\( RB+BC = 5+9.22 = 14.22 \)
\( \sqrt{202} \approx 14.21 \)
14.22 ≠ 14.21 (the values are close but not equal)
Answer
∴ RB + BC ≠ RC, so R, B and C are NOT collinear.
NCERTQ8(i)
Using the origin as one vertex, plot a right-angled isosceles triangle.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
📌 Isosceles triangle: a triangle with exactly two equal sides.
Given
A right-angled isosceles triangle has two equal sides meeting at the right angle. Take these along the x-axis and y-axis.
Formula
Pythagoras: hypotenuse\(^2\) = (side 1)\(^2\) + (side 2)\(^2\)
Working
Let O = (0,0), A = (4,0), B = (0,4)
OA = 4 units (along x-axis), OB = 4 units (along y-axis)
\( OA \perp OB \) (x-axis is perpendicular to y-axis), so the right angle is at O
OA = OB = 4 (two equal sides → isosceles)
\( AB = \sqrt{4^2+4^2} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2} \) units
Answer
∴ O(0,0), A(4,0), B(0,4) form a right-angled isosceles triangle, right angle at O, hypotenuse \( 4\sqrt{2} \) units.
NCERTQ8(ii)
Plot an isosceles triangle with one vertex at the origin, one in Quadrant III, and one in Quadrant IV.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Given
Choose the two non-origin vertices as mirror images of each other in the y-axis (same distance from O, opposite side), so they are automatically equidistant from O.
Working
Let O = (0,0), P = (−3,−4), Q = (3,−4)
P is in Quadrant III (x < 0, y < 0). Q is in Quadrant IV (x > 0, y < 0)
\( OP = \sqrt{3^2+4^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \) units
\( OQ = \sqrt{3^2+4^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \) units
\( OP = OQ = 5 \) (⇒ isosceles)
Answer
∴ O(0,0), P(−3,−4), Q(3,−4) form an isosceles triangle; OP = OQ = 5 units.
NCERTQ9
For each row, state whether M is the midpoint of segment ST.
Ask yourself: When is M really the midpoint of ST?
Given
M is the midpoint of ST only if SM = MT (checked with the distance formula, or the pattern \(x_1+x_2=2M_x\), \(y_1+y_2=2M_y\)).
Formula
\[ d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2} \]
SMTMidpoint?
(−3,0)(0,0)(3,0)YES
(2,3)(3,4)(4,5)YES
(0,0)(0,5)(0,−10)NO
(−8,7)(0,−2)(6,−3)NO
Working (Row 3)
S(0,0), M(0,5), T(0,−10)
\( SM = \sqrt{(0-0)^2+(5-0)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \)
\( MT = \sqrt{(0-0)^2+(-10-5)^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15 \)
\( SM \neq MT \)
Working (Row 4)
S(−8,7), M(0,−2), T(6,−3)
\( SM = \sqrt{(0-(-8))^2+(-2-7)^2} = \sqrt{64+81} = \sqrt{145} \)
\( MT = \sqrt{(6-0)^2+(-3-(-2))^2} = \sqrt{36+1} = \sqrt{37} \)
\( SM \neq MT \)
Answer
∴ Rows 1 and 2: M is the midpoint. Rows 3 and 4: M is NOT the midpoint (SM ≠ MT in each case).
NCERTQ10
M(−7,1) is the midpoint of A(3,−4) and B(x,y). Find B.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Ask yourself: We know the midpoint and one endpoint — how do we find the other endpoint?
Formula
\[ x_2 = 2M_x - x_1, \qquad y_2 = 2M_y - y_1 \]
Working
x-coordinate of B: \( x = 2(-7) - 3 = -14-3 = -17 \)
y-coordinate of B: \( y = 2(1) - (-4) = 2+4 = 6 \)
Answer
∴ B = (−17, 6)
NCERTQ11
P, Q trisect AB (P closer to A). Find P and Q for A(4,7) and B(16,−2).
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
📌 Trisect: to divide a line segment into 3 equal parts. P and Q below are the two trisection points.
Ask yourself: What shortcut can we use, instead of finding P and Q the long way?
Given
P is 1/3 of the way from A to B; Q is 2/3 of the way.
Working
Total change in x: \( 16-4=12 \). Each third = \( 12/3 = 4 \)
P: x = 4+4 = 8. Q: x = 4+8 = 12
Total change in y: \( -2-7=-9 \). Each third = \( -9/3 = -3 \)
P: y = 7+(−3) = 4. Q: y = 7+(−6) = 1
Answer
∴ P = (8, 4), Q = (12, 1)
NCERTQ12(i)
Show that A(1,−8), B(−4,7), C(−7,−4) lie on a circle K centred at the origin. Find the radius.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Ask yourself: When do several points all lie on the same circle?
Given
All points on a circle are equidistant from the centre — check OA, OB, OC.
Working
\( OA = \sqrt{1^2+(-8)^2} = \sqrt{1+64} = \sqrt{65} \)
\( OB = \sqrt{(-4)^2+7^2} = \sqrt{16+49} = \sqrt{65} \)
\( OC = \sqrt{(-7)^2+(-4)^2} = \sqrt{49+16} = \sqrt{65} \)
\( OA = OB = OC = \textcolor{#B03030}{\sqrt{65}} \)
Answer
∴ A, B, C lie on circle K centred at O(0,0), with radius \( \sqrt{65} \) units.
NCERTQ12(ii)
Check whether D(−5,6) and E(0,9) lie inside, on, or outside circle K.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Given
Radius of K = \( \sqrt{65} \approx 8.06 \). Compare each point's distance from O with the radius.
Working
\( OD = \sqrt{(-5)^2+6^2} = \sqrt{25+36} = \sqrt{61} \approx 7.81 \)
\( \sqrt{61} < \sqrt{65} \) (distance < radius ⇒ inside)
\( OE = \sqrt{0^2+9^2} = \sqrt{81} = 9 \)
\( 9 > \sqrt{65} \) (distance > radius ⇒ outside)
Answer
∴ D(−5,6) lies INSIDE circle K. E(0,9) lies OUTSIDE circle K.
NCERTQ13
D(5,1), E(6,5), F(0,3) are the midpoints of the sides of triangle ABC. Find A, B, C.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
📌 Medial triangle: the triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of another triangle. D, E, F here are midpoints, not vertices.
Ask yourself: How do we use midpoint information to find the original vertices?
Given
Let A\((x_1,y_1)\), B\((x_2,y_2)\), C\((x_3,y_3)\). D is midpoint of BC, E is midpoint of CA, F is midpoint of AB.
Formula
\[ M = \left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right) \]
Working — setting up equations
D(5,1) = midpoint of BC: \( x_2+x_3=10 \), \( y_2+y_3=2 \)
E(6,5) = midpoint of CA: \( x_3+x_1=12 \), \( y_3+y_1=10 \)
F(0,3) = midpoint of AB: \( x_1+x_2=0 \), \( y_1+y_2=6 \)
Working — solving x
From \( x_1+x_2=0 \): \( x_2=-x_1 \)
Substitute in \( x_2+x_3=10 \): \( -x_1+x_3=10 \) so \( x_3=10+x_1 \)
Substitute in \( x_3+x_1=12 \): \( 10+x_1+x_1=12 \) so \( 2x_1=2 \) so \( x_1=1 \)
\( x_2=-1 \), \( x_3=11 \)
Working — solving y
From \( y_1+y_2=6 \): \( y_2=6-y_1 \)
Substitute in \( y_2+y_3=2 \): \( 6-y_1+y_3=2 \) so \( y_3=y_1-4 \)
Substitute in \( y_3+y_1=10 \): \( y_1-4+y_1=10 \) so \( 2y_1=14 \) so \( y_1=7 \)
\( y_2=-1 \), \( y_3=3 \)
Answer
∴ A = (1, 7), B = (−1, −1), C = (11, 3)
NCERTQ14
A city has 10 N–S and 10 E–W streets, 200 m apart, using the convention (N–S street no., E–W street no.). How many intersections can be called (4,3), and how many (3,4)?
Working
(4,3) = the 4th N–S street meeting the 3rd E–W street — exactly one such crossing exists
(3,4) = the 3rd N–S street meeting the 4th E–W street — exactly one such crossing exists, and it is a different crossing from (4,3)
Answer
∴ (a) Only 1 intersection can be called (4,3). (b) Only 1 intersection can be called (3,4). These are different intersections — order matters.
NCERTQ15
A 800×600 px screen has origin at the bottom-left. Circle A: centre (100,150), radius 80. Circle B: centre (250,230), radius 100. (i) Does either circle go outside the screen? (ii) Do the circles intersect?
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Working — Part (i): Circle A
Left edge: 100 − 80 = 20 ≥ 0
Right edge: 100 + 80 = 180 ≤ 800
Bottom edge: 150 − 80 = 70 ≥ 0
Top edge: 150 + 80 = 230 ≤ 600
Working — Part (i): Circle B
Left edge: 250 − 100 = 150 ≥ 0
Right edge: 250 + 100 = 350 ≤ 800
Bottom edge: 230 − 100 = 130 ≥ 0
Top edge: 230 + 100 = 330 ≤ 600
Working — Part (ii)
\( AB = \sqrt{(250-100)^2+(230-150)^2} = \sqrt{150^2+80^2} = \sqrt{22500+6400} = \sqrt{28900} = 170 \) px
Sum of radii = 80 + 100 = 180 px
170 < 180 (distance between centres < sum of radii ⇒ circles overlap)
Answer
∴ (i) No part of either circle lies outside the screen. (ii) Yes, the two circles intersect each other.
NCERTQ16
Plot A(2,1), B(−1,2), C(−2,−1), D(1,−2). Is ABCD a square? Find its area.
✎ Example sketch — one possible answer (not from the textbook)
Given
A quadrilateral is a square if all four sides are equal AND both diagonals are equal.
Working — sides
\( AB = \sqrt{(-1-2)^2+(2-1)^2} = \sqrt{9+1} = \sqrt{10} \)
\( BC = \sqrt{(-2-(-1))^2+(-1-2)^2} = \sqrt{1+9} = \sqrt{10} \)
\( CD = \sqrt{(1-(-2))^2+(-2-(-1))^2} = \sqrt{9+1} = \sqrt{10} \)
\( DA = \sqrt{(2-1)^2+(1-(-2))^2} = \sqrt{1+9} = \sqrt{10} \)
All four sides = \( \textcolor{#B03030}{\sqrt{10}} \)
Working — diagonals
\( AC = \sqrt{(-2-2)^2+(-1-1)^2} = \sqrt{16+4} = \sqrt{20} \)
\( BD = \sqrt{(1-(-1))^2+(-2-2)^2} = \sqrt{4+16} = \sqrt{20} \)
Both diagonals = \( \textcolor{#B03030}{\sqrt{20}} \)
Area = side\(^2\) = \( (\sqrt{10})^2 = 10 \) sq units
Answer
∴ ABCD is a square (all sides equal and both diagonals equal). Area = 10 square units.
